options.a: Flow compressed shop air through the tubing while heating
options.b: Flow dry nitrogen through the tubing while heating
options.c: Pressurize the line with nitrogen to 150 psig while heating
options.d: Purge with nitrogen first, then braze with the flow off

distractorExplanations.a: Shop air carries oxygen and moisture, so copper oxide scale still forms inside the tube; only an inert gas such as dry nitrogen prevents it.
distractorExplanations.c: Brazing needs a low-flow nitrogen sweep of a few SCFH; a static 150 psig charge is pressure-test level and blows filler out of the open joint.
distractorExplanations.d: A pre-purge alone lets air back in as the tube heats; nitrogen must keep flowing during heating to stop oxide scale from forming.

options.a: Venting is allowed for HFC blends but illegal for CFCs and HCFCs
options.b: Recovery is required only when the system holds over 5 lb of charge
options.c: Venting regulated refrigerants to atmosphere is illegal and unsafe
options.d: Venting is legal once the system is pulled down to 0 psig first

distractorExplanations.a: The Section 608 venting prohibition covers HFC substitutes such as R-410A as well as CFCs and HCFCs; only de minimis releases are allowed.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the 5 lb small-appliance size limit with a recovery threshold; recovery is required before opening any charged system.
distractorExplanations.d: Bleeding a system to 0 psig is venting, not recovery; EPA requires certified recovery equipment to reach the required evacuation level.

options.a: Run the furnace a full cycle to see whether the smell clears up
options.b: Switch on the furnace blower to air out the room, then find the leak
options.c: Check the flue for a blockage, since that odor means flue-gas spillage
options.d: Shut the gas, ventilate, and treat it as a leak until proved otherwise

distractorExplanations.a: Operating burners and controls in a gas-odor area risks ignition; the odor itself means shut off the gas and ventilate first.
distractorExplanations.b: Operating switches or motors can spark and ignite gas; ventilate by opening doors and windows with the gas off and nothing switched.
distractorExplanations.c: The rotten-egg mercaptan odor signals unburned natural gas or propane, not combustion-product spillage, which is largely odorless CO.

options.a: Combustion air, CO awareness, and an exit plan before starting
options.b: A dust respirator, which also filters carbon monoxide safely
options.c: Sealing combustion-air openings so the attic stays conditioned
options.d: A spotter outside, with CO checks needed only for sealed boilers

distractorExplanations.b: Particulate respirators do not filter CO; CO risk is handled with ventilation, combustion air, and monitoring, not a dust mask.
distractorExplanations.c: Blocking combustion air starves the appliance and raises CO production; adequate combustion air is a requirement, not an option.
distractorExplanations.d: Any fuel-burning appliance in an enclosed attic or crawl can produce CO; CO awareness is not limited to boilers.

options.a: Replaced with the same MFD and any lower voltage rating that fits
options.b: Replaced with the specified MFD and voltage rating after discharge
options.c: Replaced with a higher MFD rating to give the motor more torque
options.d: Left in service if it still tests within 6 percent of its MFD rating

distractorExplanations.a: A lower voltage rating than the original can fail early; the replacement voltage rating must equal or exceed the original.
distractorExplanations.c: Oversizing run-capacitor MFD raises start-winding current and heat; the replacement must match the specified MFD within tolerance.
distractorExplanations.d: A bulging or cracked case means the dielectric has failed or vented; a passing MFD reading does not make a damaged capacitor safe.

options.a: A standard R-22 recovery tank, since the fittings match
options.b: A recovery machine discharging into a disposable cylinder
options.c: A recovery machine and tank rated for R-410A pressures
options.d: A vacuum pump that discharges into a recovery tank

distractorExplanations.a: Older R-22 recovery tanks may be rated below the 400 psig service pressure needed for R-410A; matching fittings say nothing about the rating.
distractorExplanations.b: Disposable DOT-39 cylinders are non-refillable; recovered refrigerant must go into a refillable, DOT-rated recovery cylinder.
distractorExplanations.d: A vacuum pump is an evacuation tool, not a recovery device; it exhausts to atmosphere and cannot push refrigerant into a pressurized tank.

options.a: An indoor-rated cord, since the condensing unit is already grounded
options.b: A heavy-gauge outdoor cord on a standard receptacle, since GFCI is for indoor wet areas
options.c: A cord with its ground pin removed so the GFCI does not nuisance-trip
options.d: Avoided; use a GFCI-protected, outdoor-rated cord only if temporary power is required

distractorExplanations.a: Indoor cords are not rated for wet outdoor exposure, and the unit's equipment ground does not protect the person handling the cord.
distractorExplanations.b: Temporary power in wet outdoor locations needs GFCI protection too; conductor gauge sizes current, it does not protect against ground faults.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the ground pin defeats the equipment grounding path; a tripping GFCI is reporting leakage that must be found and fixed.

options.a: Check defrost control, sensors, and airflow before adding charge
options.b: Add refrigerant until the outdoor coil defrosts, since icing means low charge
options.c: Switch to emergency heat and leave the outdoor unit iced until spring
options.d: Replace the reversing valve, since it fails to shift into defrost

distractorExplanations.b: Icing has several causes (failed defrost, bad sensor, low airflow); charging to melt ice without diagnosis usually overcharges the system.
distractorExplanations.c: Emergency heat is a temporary bridge; a solidly iced coil points to a defrost failure that needs repair, not seasonal abandonment.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumps to a costly part; the defrost board, coil sensor, and airflow are checked before condemning the reversing valve.

options.a: Acceptable with R-410A, because A1 refrigerants are nonflammable
options.b: An ignition hazard — remove fuels and ventilate before work
options.c: A minor risk handled by keeping a fire extinguisher within reach
options.d: Safe if the garage door is open, since vapors disperse quickly

distractorExplanations.a: The refrigerant's A1 safety class is irrelevant here; the gasoline vapor near a spark is the ignition hazard.
distractorExplanations.c: An extinguisher is a backup, not a control; the hazard is removed by taking fuels out and ventilating before any spark-producing work.
distractorExplanations.d: Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and pools near the floor; an open door does not reliably clear it from a spark source.

options.a: Safety glasses for brazing, with gloves skipped during recovery
options.b: A face shield for brazing, but no eye protection for recovery work
options.c: Eye protection, gloves, and burn protection as the task requires
options.d: Hearing protection and a hard hat, which cover recovery and brazing

distractorExplanations.a: Liquid refrigerant released at a hose connection can cause frostbite; gloves are needed during recovery as well as brazing.
distractorExplanations.b: Refrigerant spray from a hose or valve can injure the eyes; eye protection is needed when connecting hoses and recovering.
distractorExplanations.d: These protect against noise and falling objects, not refrigerant frostbite, eye splash, or torch burns.

options.a: Protect the compressor from overcurrent in place of the branch breaker
options.b: Cut 24 V control power to the unit while leaving line voltage live
options.c: Reset the compressor's internal overload after a high-amp trip
options.d: Isolate the equipment so it can be serviced without remote re-energizing

distractorExplanations.a: A non-fused disconnect gives no overcurrent protection; the branch breaker or fuses do that, and the disconnect's job is isolation.
distractorExplanations.b: The disconnect opens line voltage to the condensing unit; killing only 24 V control power leaves lethal voltage at the contactor.
distractorExplanations.c: Internal overloads reset on their own once the motor cools; the disconnect exists for lockable isolation during service.

options.a: Stop, find the blockage or heat-exchanger/vent problem, then reset only after repair
options.b: Reset the rollout switch and watch two cycles; replace it if it trips again
options.c: Raise manifold pressure so the flame pulls back into the heat exchanger
options.d: Replace the rollout switch with a higher-temperature rating so it stops tripping

distractorExplanations.b: A tripping rollout switch is usually doing its job; replacing it ignores the blocked flue or cracked heat exchanger behind the trip.
distractorExplanations.c: Higher gas pressure overfires the burner and worsens rollout; rollout comes from blocked venting or heat-exchanger problems.
distractorExplanations.d: Upsizing the limit rating defeats a flame-safety device and hides the vent or heat-exchanger problem that caused the trip.

options.a: Uncapped with valves open so any leftover vapor can vent safely
options.b: Capped, upright, and within their pressure rating, away from heat
options.c: Lying on their side in the van near the torch kit for easy access
options.d: Refilled with recovered refrigerant if they are disposable DOT-39 types

distractorExplanations.a: Open valves let moisture in and release residual refrigerant illegally; empty cylinders are stored with valves closed and caps on.
distractorExplanations.c: Cylinders stored near heat sources can overpressurize; they belong upright, secured, and away from torches and heat.
distractorExplanations.d: DOT-39 disposable cylinders are illegal to refill; empties are recovered to a vacuum, rendered unusable, and recycled.

options.a: Measuring superheat during the charge that follows evacuation
options.b: Measuring how fast the recovery machine pulls the system to 0 psig
options.c: Confirming the system is dry and leak-tight at a deep vacuum
options.d: Showing the pump's blank-off reading so the decay test can be skipped

distractorExplanations.a: Superheat needs suction pressure and line temperature with the system running; a micron gauge reads only deep vacuum.
distractorExplanations.b: The recovery endpoint is read on the manifold in psig or inches Hg; the micron gauge is for the evacuation and dehydration level.
distractorExplanations.d: Blank-off proves only the pump; a system decay test is still needed to show the circuit is dry and leak-tight.

options.a: Suction-line temperature minus saturated suction temperature
options.b: Saturated suction temperature minus suction-line temperature
options.c: Saturated condensing temperature minus liquid-line temperature
options.d: Return-air temperature minus supply-air temperature at the coil

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the subtraction; superheat is how far the actual suction-line temperature sits above saturation, a positive value.
distractorExplanations.c: That is subcooling, measured on the liquid line, not superheat measured on the suction line.
distractorExplanations.d: That is the air-side temperature split (delta T) across the coil, not refrigerant superheat.

options.a: Suction-line temperature minus saturated suction temperature
options.b: Saturated condensing temperature minus liquid-line temperature
options.c: Liquid-line temperature minus saturated condensing temperature
options.d: Discharge-line temperature minus saturated condensing temperature

distractorExplanations.a: That formula is superheat on the suction line; subcooling is taken on the liquid line against condensing saturation.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the subtraction; a properly subcooled liquid line is colder than saturation, so this order gives a negative number.
distractorExplanations.d: That is discharge superheat leaving the compressor, not subcooling of the liquid leaving the condenser.

options.a: Read deep vacuum in microns to confirm dehydration during evacuation
options.b: Measure total external static pressure across the air handler
options.c: Convert pressures to saturation and compute superheat or subcooling
options.d: Weigh the refrigerant charge added to the system during charging

distractorExplanations.a: Manifold compound gauges cannot resolve microns; a dedicated micron gauge is used to confirm dehydration.
distractorExplanations.b: TESP is measured with a manometer and static probes in the ductwork, not with a refrigerant manifold.
distractorExplanations.d: Weighing in charge uses a refrigerant scale; the manifold reads pressures and line temperatures.

options.a: Manifold gas pressure in psig, about 3.5 psig for natural gas
options.b: Deep-vacuum level in microns during line-set evacuation
options.c: Flue-gas CO in parts per million at the draft hood
options.d: Manifold or inlet gas pressure in inches of water column

distractorExplanations.a: Natural-gas manifold pressure is about 3.5 inches of water column, not 3.5 psig; psig gauges lack the needed resolution.
distractorExplanations.b: Microns are read with a micron gauge during evacuation; a furnace manometer reads gas pressure in inches WC.
distractorExplanations.c: CO in ppm is read with a combustion analyzer; a manometer measures pressure, not gas concentration.

options.a: Across the air handler, supply plus return, with the blower running
options.b: At the supply plenum only, with the blower running on high speed
options.c: Across the air handler with the blower off, to get a stable reading
options.d: Across the air handler with the filter removed for a clean baseline

distractorExplanations.b: Supply static alone leaves out the return side; TESP is the sum of supply and return static magnitudes at the air handler.
distractorExplanations.c: Static pressure exists only with airflow; with the blower off the reading is zero and tells you nothing about the duct system.
distractorExplanations.d: TESP is measured as the system operates, filter included; pulling the filter gives a falsely low reading.

options.a: 250 CFM per ton, the standard for humid-climate dehumidification
options.b: 400 CFM per ton, verified by temperature split or static
options.c: 550 CFM per ton, the usual target for heat pumps in heating mode
options.d: 800 CFM per ton, which keeps the coil from freezing in cooling

distractorExplanations.a: Humid-climate setups lower airflow to roughly 350 CFM per ton; 250 is far too low and risks a frozen evaporator coil.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat pumps also target about 400 CFM per ton; 550 overshoots it and lowers delivered supply-air temperature in heating.
distractorExplanations.d: Double the target airflow ruins dehumidification and raises static and noise; coil freezing is prevented at about 400, not 800.

nate-core-readiness-check-tools-022.explanation: 400 CFM/ton is a starting point — confirm with instruments. This item asks: “A rule-of-thumb residential airflow target is about:”. The matching answer is: 400 CFM per ton, verified by temperature split or static, not guessed. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Verify the airflow by measurement; it should not be guessed.

options.a: Measure winding resistance to ground after a compressor burnout
options.b: Compare running amps to the LRA rating to confirm normal operation
options.c: Compare running amps to the RLA/FLA nameplate under load
options.d: Measure compressor winding resistance between C, S, and R

distractorExplanations.a: Insulation resistance to ground is a megohmmeter test with power off, not a clamp-on ammeter reading.
distractorExplanations.b: LRA is the locked-rotor inrush figure, several times running current; running amps are compared to RLA, not LRA.
distractorExplanations.d: Winding resistance is an ohmmeter test with power off; a clamp-on ammeter measures current under load.

options.a: Dew point of the refrigerant to calculate system subcooling
options.b: Duct static pressure to find a restricted return or dirty filter
options.c: Flue-gas temperature and oxygen to set combustion efficiency
options.d: Wet-bulb/dry-bulb or enthalpy to diagnose airflow and capacity

distractorExplanations.a: Subcooling uses refrigerant pressure and liquid-line temperature; a psychrometer measures moisture in the air stream.
distractorExplanations.b: Duct static pressure is read with a manometer; a psychrometer reads air temperature and humidity.
distractorExplanations.c: Flue-gas temperature and O2 are measured with a combustion analyzer, not a psychrometric probe.

options.a: Weight, staying under the cylinder’s rated fill limit
options.b: Weight, filling to 100 percent of the rated water capacity
options.c: Pressure, stopping when the tank reaches 80 percent of its rating
options.d: Sight glass, stopping when liquid appears in the vapor valve

distractorExplanations.b: Recovery cylinders may be filled to only about 80 percent of capacity so liquid has room to expand; 100 percent risks rupture.
distractorExplanations.c: Cylinder pressure follows temperature, not liquid level; the fill limit is set by weight, not by a pressure reading.
distractorExplanations.d: Liquid at the vapor valve means the cylinder is already overfilled with no vapor space left for expansion.

options.a: Measure running amps against the nameplate RLA under load
options.b: Check winding insulation resistance to ground after a burnout
options.c: Measure winding-to-winding resistance between C, S, and R
options.d: Check run capacitor microfarads before a compressor restart

distractorExplanations.a: Running amps versus RLA is a clamp-on ammeter check; a megohmmeter tests insulation with the motor de-energized.
distractorExplanations.c: Winding-to-winding resistance is a low-ohm ohmmeter test; the megohmmeter applies high voltage to test insulation to ground.
distractorExplanations.d: Microfarads are read with a capacitance meter; a megohmmeter measures insulation resistance in megohms.

options.a: A cracked heat exchanger mixing return air into the supply
options.b: A clogged condensate drain pan backing water onto the coil
options.c: Low airflow or an undercharged/underperforming coil
options.d: A correctly working system, since low splits mean high efficiency

distractorExplanations.a: A cracked heat exchanger is a gas-furnace combustion hazard in heating; it is not what lowers a cooling temperature split.
distractorExplanations.b: A clogged drain causes overflow or a float-switch trip, not a far-too-low air temperature split across the coil.
distractorExplanations.d: A typical cooling split is roughly 16-22 °F; a very low split signals reduced capacity, not high efficiency.

nate-core-readiness-check-tools-027.explanation: A small split is an air-side or capacity problem, not an automatic gas-furnace fault. This item asks: “A temperature split (return vs supply) that is far too low on a cooling system often means:”. The matching answer is: Low airflow or an undercharged/underperforming coil — measure before adding gas. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Measure before adding gas.

options.a: Pressure drop that signals restriction or dirty media
options.b: Airflow in CFM directly, without any fan or filter table
options.c: Refrigerant-side pressure drop across the evaporator coil
options.d: Total external static pressure for the whole duct system

distractorExplanations.b: A manometer reads pressure; converting it to CFM requires a manufacturer fan or coil table, or a flow hood.
distractorExplanations.c: A water-column manometer reads the air side; refrigerant-side pressure drop needs refrigerant gauges.
distractorExplanations.d: TESP is supply plus return static at the air handler; a drop across one coil or filter is only that component's share.

options.a: Standard white PTFE plumbing tape, applied to flare fittings too
options.b: A listed gas-rated compound or tape, used on the correct threads
options.c: Refrigerant POE oil, which lubricates and seals the threads
options.d: Any pipe dope, applied to the female threads for best coverage

distractorExplanations.a: Flare fittings seal metal to metal and get no sealant, and gas threads need a gas-rated (yellow) tape, not plain PTFE.
distractorExplanations.c: POE oil is used on refrigerant flare faces and O-rings; it is not a listed sealant for gas pipe threads.
distractorExplanations.d: The compound must be gas-listed and goes on the male threads so excess is not pushed into the gas line.

options.a: Specified microfarads and a 370 V rating, even when the original is 440 V
options.b: The compressor RLA, adding about 10 MFD for each running amp
options.c: The motor’s specified microfarads and a voltage rating at or above the circuit
options.d: A higher microfarad value than specified, to boost starting torque

distractorExplanations.a: Moving from 370 V up to 440 V is acceptable, but not down; the voltage rating must equal or exceed the original.
distractorExplanations.b: No amp-to-MFD sizing rule exists; run-capacitor MFD is set by the motor design and nameplate.
distractorExplanations.d: An oversized run capacitor raises winding current and heat; extra starting torque comes from a start capacitor.

options.a: A secondary voltage of 24 V, which runs hot under normal load
options.b: An open high-pressure switch interrupting the Y circuit
options.c: A transformer rated at 40 VA serving a 20 VA control load
options.d: A shorted control circuit, stuck relay, or overloaded VA

distractorExplanations.a: 24 V is the normal secondary voltage; a correctly loaded transformer runs warm, not overheated.
distractorExplanations.b: An open switch removes load from the secondary, so the transformer runs cooler, not hotter.
distractorExplanations.c: That is half load; an oversized VA rating runs cooler, while overheating points to excess load or a short.

options.a: Before ignition to prove venting, then through the cycle as designed
options.b: After ignition is proven, to pull flue gases once the burners are lit
options.c: Only during the post-purge after the gas valve closes
options.d: In place of the circulating blower to move air through the heat exchanger

distractorExplanations.b: The inducer starts first to pre-purge and close the pressure switch; ignition is not allowed until draft is proven.
distractorExplanations.c: Post-purge is one part of its cycle, but the inducer also pre-purges and runs throughout the burn.
distractorExplanations.d: The inducer moves combustion products through the heat exchanger; the circulating blower moves conditioned air over it.

options.a: Filed smooth and returned to service as routine maintenance
options.b: Replaced; pitted contacts add resistance and drop voltage
options.c: Left in service unless the coil reads open on an ohmmeter
options.d: Kept and paired with a hard-start kit to overcome the voltage drop

distractorExplanations.a: Filing strips the contact plating and is only a temporary fix; badly pitted contactors are replaced.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses coil failure with contact wear; coil continuity says nothing about resistance across pitted contacts.
distractorExplanations.d: A hard-start kit masks the symptom by adding start torque while the pitted contacts keep degrading.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-034.explanation: Pitted contacts are a replace item, not a permanent field repair. This item asks: “A contactor with badly pitted points should be:”. The matching answer is: Replaced; pitted contacts add resistance and drop voltage to the compressor. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. That voltage drop reaches the compressor and stresses it.

options.a: Continuously, in series with the start winding like a run capacitor
options.b: During start and run, wired in parallel with the run capacitor
options.c: Only during start, dropped out by a relay or PTC once the motor is up
options.d: Only after the motor reaches speed, to correct its power factor

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a run capacitor; start capacitors are not rated for continuous duty and fail if left in circuit.
distractorExplanations.b: Hard-start capacitors connect in parallel with the run capacitor but must drop out; left in during run they overheat.
distractorExplanations.d: Running power-factor correction is the run capacitor's role; the start capacitor adds torque during start.

options.a: In heating on every brand, because the valve fails safe to cooling
options.b: By 240 V line voltage from the contactor whenever the compressor runs
options.c: In both modes, with defrost switching the valve off to reverse flow
options.d: In one mode (often cooling) depending on the OEM — check the wiring diagram

distractorExplanations.a: Some brands energize the valve in heating (B terminal) but most energize in cooling (O); it varies by OEM.
distractorExplanations.b: The reversing-valve solenoid is a 24 V coil fed from the thermostat O/B circuit, not line voltage tied to the compressor.
distractorExplanations.c: The valve is energized in only one mode; defrost puts it into the cooling position, which may be on or off by brand.

options.a: Inducer, vent/intake, and the hose to the switch
options.b: The flame sensor, since it proves the pressure switch
options.c: The high limit switch and the blower wheel for dust
options.d: The gas valve outlet pressure with a manometer

distractorExplanations.b: The flame sensor proves flame after ignition; a pressure-switch fault is about inducer draft before ignition.
distractorExplanations.c: A high-limit trip is a different fault code; a pressure-switch fault points to the inducer and venting.
distractorExplanations.d: The gas valve is not energized until the pressure switch closes, so testing it first skips the draft circuit.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-037.explanation: Pressure-switch faults are venting/inducer problems until proved otherwise. This item asks: “If a furnace control flashes a pressure-switch fault, first check:”. The matching answer is: Inducer, vent/intake, and the hose to the switch — not the gas valve first. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Check those before suspecting the gas valve.

options.a: Normal inrush that settles within a few minutes
options.b: The compressor or fan motor is not starting
options.c: A high-efficiency scroll running at full capacity
options.d: A normal reading during the defrost cycle

distractorExplanations.a: Normal inrush lasts well under a second; LRA that does not drop means the rotor is locked.
distractorExplanations.c: A motor at full load draws about RLA, far below locked-rotor amps.
distractorExplanations.d: Defrost does not make the compressor draw locked-rotor amps; running current stays near RLA.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-038.explanation: LRA that never falls is a failed start, not a running load. This item asks: “A clamp meter showing locked-rotor amps that do not drop means:”. The matching answer is: The compressor or fan motor is not starting — stop and diagnose mechanical/electrical start. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Stop and diagnose the mechanical or electrical start problem.

options.a: 24 V hot and the cooling call to the contactor
options.b: 120 V hot and neutral from the furnace transformer
options.c: 24 V hot and common for the control circuit
options.d: 24 V hot and the reversing-valve output

distractorExplanations.a: The cooling call to the contactor is Y; C is the common return of the 24 V transformer secondary.
distractorExplanations.b: 120 V feeds the transformer primary; R and C are the 24 V secondary leads.
distractorExplanations.d: The reversing-valve output is O or B; C is the common side of the control circuit.

options.a: Be bonded to the refrigerant suction line as its ground point
options.b: Have its C terminal left disconnected to keep the secondary floating
options.c: Be grounded on both secondary legs to keep the circuit balanced
options.d: Follow the OEM grounding/C connection so safeties and Wi-Fi stats work

distractorExplanations.a: Refrigerant piping is not a control-circuit grounding point; the OEM grounding and C connection must be followed.
distractorExplanations.b: C is still needed for powered thermostats and safeties; a floating secondary still uses its common lead.
distractorExplanations.c: Grounding both secondary legs shorts the transformer through the ground path and blows the fuse.

options.a: The indoor coil reaches the termination temperature or a time limit
options.b: The outdoor coil reaches the termination temperature or a time limit
options.c: The outdoor air temperature rises above the balance point setting
options.d: The fixed 90-minute run-time interval set on the board has elapsed

distractorExplanations.a: Defrost terminates on the outdoor coil sensor; the indoor coil is not what is being defrosted.
distractorExplanations.c: The balance point governs auxiliary-heat lockout and staging, not defrost termination.
distractorExplanations.d: The 30/60/90-minute pins set the interval between defrost checks, not when an active defrost ends.

options.a: A run capacitor plus speed taps wired on the motor's line-voltage side
options.b: A variable-frequency drive mounted in the furnace's control panel
options.c: A control signal (PWM, serial, or 24 V taps) plus a correct line-voltage feed
options.d: Line voltage alone, with speed set by the motor's internal thermistor

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a PSC blower motor; ECMs have no run capacitor and are commanded by a control signal.
distractorExplanations.b: ECM drive electronics are built into the motor module; no separate panel-mounted VFD is used.
distractorExplanations.d: An ECM needs a command signal from the control; line power alone does not set its speed or torque.

options.a: Jumper R to C at the thermostat so it can draw continuous power
options.b: Power the thermostat with a plug-in 120 V adapter wired to the R and C terminals
options.c: Swap in fresh batteries, since a C-wire is just a battery backup
options.d: Add a common or an approved power extender per the furnace and stat docs

distractorExplanations.a: Jumping R to C shorts the 24 V transformer secondary and blows the control fuse or the transformer.
distractorExplanations.b: R and C are 24 V control terminals; feeding it 120 V destroys the thermostat and the furnace control.
distractorExplanations.c: A C-wire supplies continuous 24 V power; batteries do not stop a power-stealing Wi-Fi thermostat from dropping out.

options.a: Per the unit nameplate maximum fuse/breaker
options.b: At the minimum circuit ampacity printed on the nameplate
options.c: At 125 percent of the compressor RLA, ignoring fan motor loads
options.d: To the compressor's locked-rotor amps on the nameplate

distractorExplanations.b: Minimum circuit ampacity sizes the conductors; fuses are sized from the nameplate maximum overcurrent rating.
distractorExplanations.c: 125 percent of RLA is part of the MCA calculation for wire sizing, not the fuse rating.
distractorExplanations.d: LRA is far above the maximum overcurrent rating; fusing at LRA gives the circuit no real protection.

nate-core-readiness-check-electrical-045.explanation: Nameplate Max fuse / HACR breaker is the rule. This item asks: “A fused disconnect at the condensing unit should be sized:”. The matching answer is: Per the unit nameplate maximum fuse/breaker, not an arbitrary 60 A. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Do not pick an arbitrary size such as 60 A.

options.a: Add the pound, since a top-off is acceptable on residential systems
options.b: Diagnose with gauges, temperatures, and airflow before changing charge
options.c: Check suction pressure alone and add charge if it reads below 100 psig
options.d: Recover the full charge and weigh in nameplate charge before any testing

distractorExplanations.a: Adding charge without measurements can overcharge the system; the charge is set by superheat or subcooling and airflow.
distractorExplanations.c: Pressure alone cannot show charge level; superheat or subcooling needs temperatures and correct airflow too.
distractorExplanations.d: Jumping to recovery skips diagnosis; testing first shows whether charge is the problem at all.

options.a: EPA requires these records on every residential service call
options.b: NATE audits each technician's service tickets to renew the credential
options.c: The next tech and the warranty need a traceable service record
options.d: The invoice total is the only item a warranty claim requires

distractorExplanations.a: EPA recordkeeping targets disposal and larger appliances, not a full service record on every residential call.
distractorExplanations.b: NATE recertification uses continuing-education hours or retesting, not audits of service tickets.
distractorExplanations.d: Warranty claims require model, serial, and failure details; an invoice total proves nothing about the failed part.

options.a: Jumper out the failed safety so the customer has cooling overnight, then return tomorrow
options.b: Leave the system running as-is and return when the part arrives
options.c: Recover the charge and leave gauges on the ports until you return
options.d: Leave the system safe, explain options and price, and schedule the follow-up

distractorExplanations.a: Bypassing a safety control creates a hazard and liability; the system must be left in a safe state.
distractorExplanations.b: Running a faulty system can cause further damage; it should be left safe with the customer told the options.
distractorExplanations.c: Gauges left on ports invite leaks and tampering, and the customer still has no explanation, price, or schedule.

options.a: Buy and handle regulated refrigerants and perform recovery
options.b: Install line-voltage wiring to a condensing unit disconnect
options.c: Pull gas permits and install furnaces under the mechanical code
options.d: Purchase sealed refrigerant appliances like window AC units

distractorExplanations.b: Electrical wiring is governed by state and local licensing; EPA 608 covers refrigerant handling.
distractorExplanations.c: Gas permits and furnace installs fall under local mechanical licensing, not EPA 608 certification.
distractorExplanations.d: Factory-sealed appliances can be sold to anyone; 608 certification governs buying refrigerant and recovery work.

options.a: The system is over 10 years old, even if the repair is a simple capacitor
options.b: The existing equipment is unsafe or uneconomic and the facts are shown to the owner
options.c: The repair quote tops 25 percent of a new system, before diagnosis is complete
options.d: The unit uses R-22, since R-22 systems are now illegal to repair

distractorExplanations.a: Age alone does not justify replacement; a cheap repair on a sound unit should be offered first.
distractorExplanations.c: Cost rules of thumb mean nothing before diagnosis; replacement advice must rest on documented findings.
distractorExplanations.d: R-22 production ended in 2020, but servicing R-22 systems with reclaimed or stocked refrigerant is still legal.

options.a: Disregard them, since only a combustion analyzer can confirm a crack
options.b: Red-tag the furnace from the photos alone without inspecting it
options.c: Inspect, confirm, shut the furnace down if unsafe, and document in writing
options.d: Replace the heat exchanger at once, as photos are proof of a crack

distractorExplanations.a: Photos are a lead worth checking; visual or camera inspection and combustion testing together confirm a crack.
distractorExplanations.b: Condemning equipment needs the technician's own confirmation; photos alone may show a stain rather than a crack.
distractorExplanations.d: Photos can mislead; the technician inspects and confirms before shutting down or quoting a heat exchanger.

options.a: Defer to the senior tech's reading and adjust the charge to match what that tech measured
options.b: Split the difference and add half the charge each tech suggested
options.c: Go with whichever reading uses the newer digital manifold set
options.d: Re-measure SH/SC, airflow, and nameplate together before adding more gas

distractorExplanations.a: Seniority is not a measurement; the disagreement is settled by re-measuring superheat, subcooling, and airflow.
distractorExplanations.b: A compromise amount is not a diagnosis and can still leave the system over- or undercharged.
distractorExplanations.c: Tool age does not settle a charge dispute; both techs re-measure together against the nameplate.

options.a: Explain coil/blower damage and IAQ risk and leave a proper filter in place
options.b: Remove it as requested, since the customer owns the equipment
options.c: Install a MERV 16 filter so the system gets cleaner, freer airflow
options.d: Remove it and clean the coil yearly to make up for the missing filter

distractorExplanations.b: Removing the filter exposes the coil and blower to dirt; the technician should explain the risk first.
distractorExplanations.c: A high-MERV filter in a thin slot raises static pressure and reduces airflow rather than freeing it.
distractorExplanations.d: Yearly coil cleaning does not stop debris loading the blower and coil between cleanings; filtration is still needed.

options.a: Repair it yourself after hours before mentioning it to anyone
options.b: Tell the shop and the customer immediately and follow company claim policy
options.c: Report it to the shop only and let the office contact the customer about the claim later
options.d: Note it on the invoice and let the customer raise it if they notice

distractorExplanations.a: Concealing damage breaks trust and company claim procedures; the shop and customer are told right away.
distractorExplanations.c: The customer should hear about the damage from the technician immediately, not later from the office.
distractorExplanations.d: Passive disclosure on paperwork is not telling the customer; damage is reported directly and immediately.

options.a: Acceptable if the post leaves out the customer's last name
options.b: Acceptable once the job is finished and the system is paid for
options.c: A privacy failure — never post customer credentials or addresses
options.d: Acceptable if the address is blurred out of the photo

distractorExplanations.a: The PIN is still an access credential; omitting a surname does not make posting it safe.
distractorExplanations.b: Payment status does not change privacy duties; customer credentials are never posted.
distractorExplanations.d: Blurring the address leaves the PIN exposed, and the PIN itself grants control of the system.

options.a: Upsizing the breaker one size so the furnace stops nuisance-tripping
options.b: Resetting it and telling the customer to call if it trips again
options.c: Replacing the breaker, since a breaker that trips has worn out
options.d: Finding why it tripped before resetting forever and walking away

distractorExplanations.a: Breakers are sized to protect the wire; upsizing creates a fire risk and hides the fault causing the trip.
distractorExplanations.b: A trip signals an overload or fault; the cause should be found before the visit ends.
distractorExplanations.c: Breakers usually trip because of overload or short circuit; replacing one without diagnosis leaves the fault in place.

options.a: Include recovery, drier, evacuation, start components, and labor
options.b: List the compressor and labor, with recovery and drier billed later
options.c: Include the part and labor, since a new compressor ships with a drier
options.d: Include the compressor, drier, and labor, reusing the old charge

distractorExplanations.b: Billing required steps later hides the true cost; the quote should include every required line up front.
distractorExplanations.c: Replacement compressors do not ship with a filter-drier; a new drier is a separate required item.
distractorExplanations.d: Omits recovery, evacuation, and start components; the charge still has to be recovered and handled.

nate-core-readiness-check-soft-skills-05.explanation: A complete quote prevents callbacks and angry invoices. This item asks: “When quoting a compressor, the estimate should:”. The matching answer is: Include recovery, drier, evacuation, start components, and labor — not just the part. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. Quoting just the part hides required work from the customer.

options.a: Do the resize under your HVAC license if it is a short run
options.b: Stop and bring in a licensed plumber or fitter
options.c: Upsize the gas valve instead so the line can stay as installed
options.d: Do the resize and skip the permit since it is a service call

distractorExplanations.a: Gas piping work needs the specific license the jurisdiction requires; run length does not change that.
distractorExplanations.c: A larger gas valve cannot fix an undersized supply line; the piping itself must be resized.
distractorExplanations.d: Calling it a service call does not remove licensing or permit rules for gas piping work.

options.a: A state contractor license exam for HVAC installation and service work
options.b: The federal refrigerant-handling exam that replaces the EPA 608 card
options.c: An industry knowledge exam for HVAC installation and service fundamentals
options.d: A manufacturer warranty course required to install specific brands

distractorExplanations.a: NATE is a voluntary industry certification; contractor licensing is issued by states or localities.
distractorExplanations.b: EPA 608 is a separate federal requirement; NATE certification does not replace it.
distractorExplanations.d: NATE is brand-neutral and run by an independent body, not a manufacturer warranty program.

nate-core-readiness-check-soft-skills-05.explanation: NATE is a certification exam; licenses are still state-issued. This item asks: “NATE Core is best described as:”. The matching answer is: An industry knowledge exam for HVAC installation and service fundamentals — not a state license by itself. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official NATE or state operator paper. It is not a state license by itself.

options.a: Reinstalling panels and leaving gauges connected to verify the charge overnight
options.b: Removing scraps and leaving the blower door off to cool the motor
options.c: Confirming the system runs in the called mode and leaving the scraps for the homeowner to bin
options.d: Reinstalling panels, removing scraps, and confirming the system runs in the called mode

distractorExplanations.a: Gauges left on the ports create a leak path and tampering risk; they come off before the tech leaves.
distractorExplanations.b: The blower door must be reinstalled; leaving it off defeats the door switch and pulls unfiltered air.
distractorExplanations.c: Cleanup is part of the job; leaving scraps and packaging behind is unprofessional and can be a hazard.
